> > 1. breadcrumb
>

> This is not an error but the implementation according to the concept. The concept does not include a breadcrumb, and the text has been adapted according to the concept. If you want to adjust the font, you can easily do so in global.css. Please note that these are "global" changes.

Ah ok, I see.
In that case I have some sort of challenge. I used the breadcrumb as "back navigation" to jump a list back into position.
For instance go to Artists, scroll down a lot, click an artist to view details. Then if you do browser back, you get back into the artists listing but not at the scrolling position which is annoying as you need to scroll down again. So there was a bit of a workaround in the code to remember the position in the router and then when you navigate back, you scroll back to that position again where you left off.

If we can somehow reintroduce that behavior again, I don't care about the breadcrumb :-)

author: marcelveldt
body:
I'm not sure this is good;

a) there is no common format for streamtitle, radio stations just mess around.
b) like you already discovered some radio stations have jiberish in this stream title, some even put xml or json in there.
c) I'm not sure of the search is well protected

Overall the outcome will not be predictable and cause confusion. 
Maybe we can do a safeguard and only start search if there's a hyphen in the title ?
Its still no guarantee as some radio stations do TITLE -ARTIST and some others do ARTIST-TITLE and some others do just the title or a variation but at least when there's an hyphen we know almost certain its possibly a artist/title combination.
Still its hacky because some radio stations just have the show title in their or a commercial or whatever.

author: marcelveldt
body:
Closing in favor of an incremental, piece-by-piece refactor on current `main`.

The direction here (shadcn + `@tanstack/vue-form` + `zod`) was right — `main` has since adopted those exact libraries, so we're building on the same foundation. But this branch predates the i18n server-migration (it re-translates server-provided strings on the frontend, which is now resolved server-side), uses the old icon package (`lucide-vue-next` vs `@lucide/vue`), and conflicts with several config changes that have landed since. Rather than rebase the whole 14-file change at once, we're redoing it in small, reviewable PRs.

Salvaged from here for the later steps: the `config-entry.ts` zod/validation helpers, the `ConfigEntryRow` split, and the shadcn `alert` component.

Thanks @stvncode — this was a useful blueprint. 🙏

First step just landed: #2008

author: marcelveldt
body:
this is a bit weird to use a contextmanager. I was under the impression that you needed to validate the session each call. In that case you can perhaps store the session as attribute on your class instance and use the contextmanager on every call that needs the session. Within the context manager you can then perform a quick check if the token needs to be refreshed, cleanup resources etc.

There is no actual need for a contextmanager but its just comfortable. You can even turn a method within your class into a contextmanager: https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextlib.html#contextlib.asynccontextmanager

so you can store/cache the session as instance attribute.
and then in every function that needs access to the session you do something like this:

session = self.get_tidal_session()
and then do something with that session

or the contextmanager approach:

async with self.get_tidal_session() as session:
   session.do_something()

and in the "get_tidal_session" you do all the checks needed if the session is still valid, auth token fresh etc.

You can also create a decorator and decorate all functions.

or the lazy approach is to just call whatever on the todil session and catch the exception that the token expired, refresh it then and then retry.

So enough approaches ;-)

body:
Yeah, you just need to make sure to grab each segment, yield chunks and then grab next segment yield chunks and so on. We have some helpers in the audio.py module to help with parsing the m3u file if you want that.

and yes, you need to yield the smaller chunks otherwise it will all be loaded in memory
Basically you just reimplement the "get_segment" function from the lib but instead of returning the resp.content, you just yield chunks from the resp.iter_any or resp.iter_chunked

So something along these lines within the get_audio_stream:

```
playlist_file = get_sirius_playlist_m3u8_file
playlist_segments = parse_playlist_into_the segment_parts

for playlist_segment in playlist_segments:
    url = urllib.parse.urljoin(await self.get_hls_root(), path)
    res = await self._session.get(url, params=self._token_params())

        if res.status_code == 403:
            raise SegmentRetrievalException(
                "Received status code 403 on segment, renew session"
            )

        if res.is_error:
            self._log.warn(f"Received status code {res.status_code} on segment")
            return None

        for chunk in res.iter_any():
            yield chunk

```

You could try first by just using the entire contents from the get_segment function btw, maybe its not that big

Well we do not want the recently played tracks as a source for our radio. We only want to use the _originally enqueued media items_ as a source for the radio, because they represent the closest of what the user intended to play. 

The logic here checks if we are playing the last item in the queue and, if DSTM is enabled, uses those _originally enqueued media items_ as a radio source to dynamically fill the queue.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
> Sure but radio mode is always based on the tracks right ? So radio mode for playlist --> will be based on the tracks So radio mode for album--> will be based on the tracks

No, radio mode is based on `MediaItems`. So the `radio_source` can be a list of let's say `[Album, Track, Playlist]`. The radio _logic_ translates this into a list of base tracks (random 5 tracks per `MediaItem`), in this case 5 album tracks + the enqueued track + 5 random playlist tracks. Then it will create the dynamic playlist based on similar tracks for all of those base tracks.

This ensures that the originally enqueued items are remembered so we can always go back to them for generating a fresh list of dynamic tracks. This prevents the 'algorithm' to deviate from what was originally played.

body:
This is not the way to do this, sorry.
You will receive an uri within the MediaItemPlaybackProgressReport, which could be from SubSonic provider but it can also be a library item. In that case you need to enumerate the provider mappings of the media item to find out if one of them is from subsonic provider.

```
from music_assistant.helpers.uri import parse_uri
media_type, provider_instance_id_or_domain, item_id = await parse_uri(uri)
if provider_instance_id_or_domain == "library":
    # unwrap library item to check if we have a subsonic mapping...
    library_item = await self.mass.music.get_library_item_by_prov_id(media_type, item_id, provider_instance_id_or_domain)
    if library_item is None:
        return None
    for mapping in library_item.provider_mapings:
        ...
elif not provider_instance_id_or_domain.startswith("subsonic"):
    # not an item from subsonic provider, ignore...
    return None
```

body:
So, one thing to consider here is tha added overhead of requiring a coroutine for all these parsers.
Parsers should normally be lightweight, IO-free methods that simple take the raw data and spit out the MA model equivalent. Within such parser make sure to not do (or have the need to) make any API calls.

If your api returns incomplete data in the main listings, that is perfectly fine. If you then return the full item details within the "get_artist", "get_track" etc. methods then it can be retrieved later when its needed.

If the data is really minimal, you can also consider returning it as ItemMapping objects. Then the internal machinery will know that it needs to fetch the full object before e.g. playing or storing it.

> Ah, looking at the type hints, checksum is declared as str | None.

> You can just remove those lines since checksum is already typed as str | None and can't be anything else. If you want to ensure it's a string when not None, the type system already guarantees that.
> If the function might actually receive non-string values at runtime (despite the type hint), you'd need to change the type hint to str | None | Any or similar, but that's usually not the right approach.

author: marcelveldt
body:
problem is that you create a mapping per provider instance but a provider instance can have multiple mappings for the same item - for example a single track in spotify (or any other streaming provider) can have multiple mappings.

So I would suggest that we simply do not allow updating provider mappings at all in the update_item functions and instead we have a method to update item mappings not exposed on the api.
But at the same time we would want the provider mappings to be manageable, for example to allow a user to remove a mapping or simply link items together.

That brings us back to the real issue; we don't want to accept malicious paths to be injected through an api call. I'll have to chew on this for a little while to overthink our options.

In any case, the change you propose here isn't going to work

Error: Argument 1 to `add_item_to_library` of "MediaControllerBase" has incompatible type `Artist | ItemMapping`; expected `Artist`

body:
@kieranhogg 

I have just added stream_metadata_update_callback to the streamdetails (models bump upcoming in the server)
you can register any async (instance) method there and it will be called at each X interval with the streamdetails object at first parameter and the played seconds as second parameter

the interval can be controlled with stream_metadata_update_interval

```
StreamDetails(
    blah=blah,
    ....
    stream_metadata=StreamMetadata(initial metadata...)
    stream_metadata_update_callback = self._update_stream_metadata,
    stream_metadata_update_interval = 5  # =5 seconds
)
```

and the actual callback:
```
async def _update_stream_metadata(self, streamdetails: StreamDetails, elapsed_time: int) -> None:
    # do check if metadata needs to be updated
    # if needed, simply update the metadata fields here
    streamdetails.stream_metadata.title = blah etc
```

elapsed_time in this case will be the actual elapsed time and not the "seconds streamed" which can be a bit ahead due to buffering.

Hope this is useful this way!

@OzGav also FYI as you wanted to do something similar for the Pandora provider I believe ?

body:
Yeah my Grease case was still OK as it had all the required tags but yes in cases where there was only a an ARTIST tag then ambiguity is there. So I have beefed up the logic to handle many edge cases.

The MusicBrainz Artist ID count is the source of truth for how many artists to extract from the ARTIST tag. Ideally an ARTISTS tag is used.
Logic:
  1. ARTISTS tag present → Split on ;, use all results (unchanged)
  2. ARTIST tag with MB Artist IDs:
    - 0 IDs: Only split on "featuring" splitters (feat., featuring, ft., duet with, vs.), never on &, ,, +, or with
    - 1 ID: Return as-is, no splitting at all
    - 2+ IDs: Split on featuring splitters first, then split on extra splitters (&, ,, +, with) only until we reach the MB
  ID count — then stop
  3. Warnings: Logged when we can't match the expected count or have to stop early or when number of artists found in the ARTISTS tag does not equal the number of MB ARTIST IDs

This review comment is not particularly valid in this context. Here’s why:
	1.	The tests that import _parse_vorbis_tags are unit tests with mocked VCommentDict objects — they’re specifically testing the parsing logic in isolation, which is exactly what unit tests should do. Testing through parse_tags_mutagen or async_parse_tags would require real audio files for every edge case (multiple artist fields, precedence of ARTISTS over ARTIST, etc.), making the tests slower, more brittle, and harder to maintain.
	2.	The file already tests through the public API too — test_parse_metadata_from_flac_with_multiple_artist_fields uses async_parse_tags with a real FLAC fixture. The mock-based tests complement this by covering specific edge cases that would be tedious to create fixture files for.
	3.	The _ prefix convention in Python is a hint, not a contract. Within the same project’s test suite, testing private helpers directly is completely normal and expected. This isn’t a third-party consumer — it’s the project’s own tests.
	4.	Making _parse_vorbis_tags public just to satisfy the test import would be the wrong response — it’s genuinely an internal helper that shouldn’t be part of the module’s public API.

```
# allow_seek: bool to indicate that the content can/may be seeked
```

body:
The explicit MediaItemType | None annotation is required for mypy. Without it:

media_item = await media_controller.get_library_item_by_prov_id(...)

Infers type as: Artist | Album | Track | Radio | Playlist | Audiobook | Podcast | Genre | None (no PodcastEpisode)

Then when we assign from provider.get_item() which returns MediaItemType (includes PodcastEpisode), mypy errors:

error: Incompatible types in assignment (expression has type "... | PodcastEpisode | ...", variable has type "... | None")  [assignment]

The annotation widens the type to accept all media items including podcast episodes.

author: OzGav
body:
In practice, CastInfo.uuid should not be None according to the type hints, but we’ve seen defensive checks like this throughout the Chromecast codebase because discovery data can be incomplete or malformed at runtime (especially during transient zeroconf states). Removing the guard would reduce runtime robustness, while changing upstream CastInfo typing is outside the scope of this PR.

The ignore does not hide a logic bug here:

If uuid is truly non-optional, the branch is effectively dead but harmless.

If uuid can be None at runtime, the guard is correct and the ignore merely compensates for overly strict upstream typing.

Given the constraints of this PR (mypy fixes only, no behavioral changes), suppressing unreachable locally with a comment is the least risky option. A proper fix would require upstream type adjustments in pychromecast, which can be revisited separately.

author: OzGav
body:
This is a conscious trade-off rather than an oversight.

This handler mirrors how pychromecast has historically invoked remove_callback, where service is a zeroconf service tuple and the positional indices are stable in practice. The earlier cast() is there purely to satisfy typing; it does not change the runtime contract we’re relying on here.

Switching to cast_info for player_id / friendly_name would indeed be cleaner, but that would be a behavioral change, not just a typing fix. This PR is intentionally scoped to mypy cleanup only, and altering which source of truth we use for removal events could have subtle side effects (e.g. differences between service-level removal and cast-info state).

author: OzGav
body:
There are pros and cons here.

I understand NFS mounts can hang indefinitely if the server goes away, which would mean umount blocks and stops the MA shutdown. That’s the scenario ignore_error=True protects against.
I understand SMB is less prone to this because cifs mounts tend to time out rather than hang, but it’s arguably still a risk there too.
So I’d prefer to keep ignore_error=True here. A failed unmount during shutdown is harmless — the mount point gets cleaned up when the container restarts or the /tmp directory is cleared. A hung shutdown of MA is worse.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

Ok, let me walk through the problem we are actually fixing here so I completely understand what you are trying to do. As far as I understand it is this:

 `db_row["provider"]` current only returns "library" from the playlog, causing recommendations to be empty for users that have a user_provider_filter configured. Correct?

If that is the case, we should be able to simply move the filter inside the SQL query and then we can just blindly create an `ItemMapping` for every row we get back. Something like this:
```
SELECT p.item_id, p.media_type, p.name, p.image, p.provider
FROM playlog p
WHERE p.media_type IN ('audiobook', 'podcast_episode')
  AND p.fully_played = 0
  AND p.provider IN (<available_providers>)
  AND p.seconds_played > 0
  AND (
    CASE WHEN p.provider = 'library' THEN
      EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM provider_mappings m
              WHERE m.item_id = p.item_id AND m.media_type = p.media_type
              AND m.provider_instance IN (<user_provider_filter>))
    ELSE p.provider IN (<user_provider_filter>)
    END
  )
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
```

body:
Good point about not introducing new logic. I've made a few changes based on your feedback:

Replaced the hardcoded _DISPLAY_SUFFIXES list with a regex pattern that handles any casing/bracket variation of video/audio suffixes.

Eliminated _SEARCH_KEYWORDS entirely — the search patterns are now built directly from VERSION_PARTS (+ feat/ft), so there's a single source of truth for version keywords.

Added the missing keywords (edition, anniversary, stereo, album, bonus) to VERSION_PARTS so both `parse_title_and_version` and search cleaning benefit.

I kept `clean_title_for_display` as a separate function because it serves a different purpose than `parse_title_and_version` — for a title like "Elton John (feat. Kiki Dee) (Official Video)", the display function strips only the video suffix and preserves (feat. Kiki Dee), whereas `parse_title_and_version` would strip both since feat. is in IGNORE_TITLE_PARTS. For display purposes I think it would be better to keep the featuring credit visible.

For the config entries, you first check for pin pairing and secondly for password pairing. This could result in a race if the device requires both (not sure if this is a valid use case?).

```
if self._requires_pin_pairing():

    ...
```

```
if not candidate.is_absolute():

resolved = candidate.resolve()
storage_root = Path(self.mass.storage_path).resolve()
if not str(resolved).startswith(str(storage_root) + os.sep) and resolved != storage_root:
```

body:
Good catch — this was a real deadlock scenario. When the buffer was full and the consumer sought ahead of buffered data, both `_put` and `_get` would block on different conditions waiting for each other.

Fixed: `_put` now evicts the oldest chunk when at capacity instead of waiting, which eliminates both this deadlock and the negative-index bug from comment #2. The `_space_available` condition variable has been removed entirely.

author: marcelveldt
body: Fixed together with comment #1. The root cause was the same: discard-on-read could produce a negative `buffer_index` when the discarded chunk was exactly the one being requested. Moving eviction to `_put` eliminates this entirely — `_get` now only reads, never mutates the deque.

author: marcelveldt
body: Acknowledged as a best practice, but the risk is negligible here: the fill source is an in-memory async generator with no real I/O and `asyncio.sleep(0)` yields once per chunk. A 100ms window is very generous for 3-5 zero-byte chunks. We could await the producer task directly, but that would require exposing it or returning it from `fill()` — not worth the API change for a low-risk timing window in tests.

author: OzGav
body:
The answer is that this isn't an encoding choice made by MA — it comes from the OS/filesystem layer.

I understand that when Python's os module (or ffprobe via subprocess) encounters a filename that contains bytes that aren't valid UTF-8, it decodes those bytes using surrogateescape error handler. This is Python's way of preserving the raw bytes without losing data, but it produces surrogate characters that are not valid Unicode and cannot be re-encoded as UTF-8.

In the specific case in that discussion the filename was written on Windows using a filesystem or tool that used Windows-1252 encoding. When that file was accessed on the Linux system (inside the Docker container) via a volume mount, the kernel handed the raw bytes to Python which applied surrogateescape, producing the \udc92 surrogate.
So it's not MA choosing a different encoding — it's the filesystem handing MA a filename that was never valid UTF-8 to begin with. The guard is there because MA has no control over what filenames users put on their music drives.

body:
I have implemented this using a single comma-separated config entry, where each MPD server is entered in the format host, host:port, or host:port#password. Port defaults to 6600 if not specified.

Regarding the password — it authenticates the TCP connection to the MPD server, not the player. Every client connecting to that server uses the same password. Placing it in the player config would also create a chicken-and-egg problem: the player cannot be registered until the first connection succeeds, but the connection requires the password before the player config screen is even available. Keeping it inline with the host address avoids both issues.

author: OzGav
body:
The reason is that I learnt that manually-added radio stations are stored in two places:

  1. Config storage
  2. The database

The existing `update_item_in_library` only updates the database. For builtin radios, I believe we also need to update the config storage, otherwise:
  - The next sync would overwrite user changes with the old config values
  - URL changes wouldn't persist (the URL is the item_id in config)

Additionally, this PR supports URL changes which require updating the provider mapping's item_id, which the standard update flow doesn't handle.

If you'd prefer, we could extend the existing `_update_library_item` in `RadioController `to detect builtin provider mappings and update config there instead? What do you think?

author: OzGav
body:
The current approach with both `browse()` and `get_library_radios()` implemented is not correct. We recently standardised the radio provider pattern — if a provider declares `LIBRARY_RADIOS` and implements `get_library_radios()`, the base class handles browse automatically by calling the `get_library_*()` methods. You should not also be implementing `browse()` or declaring `BROWSE `in `SUPPORTED_FEATURES`.
The correct pattern is:

`get_library_radios()` yields all followed channels (all of them) and MA's library sync takes care of adding and removing from the library automatically
`recommendations()` is the right place to surface currently live channels since it is surfaced to the user on demand

Users therefore have all of their library from the provider in the MA library and use the search to find more.

Please remove `browse()` and remove `BROWSE` from `SUPPORTED_FEATURES`.
If you have a specific use case that genuinely requires a dedicated browse implementation that cannot be served by this pattern, please raise it and we can discuss, but our strong preference is to maintain the standardised approach across all providers."

author: OzGav
body: To be clear. You are filtering out non-live channels but this method is only called on each full sync of the library at the specified interval, so that could be hours old. A channel that was live when the sync ran will appear in the library, and one that wasn't live will be missing — even though the user follows both. The live status enrichment (viewer count in the name, live thumbnail) will also be stale by the time the user sees it, so it has no value here. The library should be a stable list of all followed channels with basic profile info and nothing more.

body:
The moving target is intentional and correct here. Both `min_position` and `seconds_streamed` advance at the same rate (~1s/s), so the relative gap stays constant - once the buffer catches up, the condition becomes true.

Freezing `min_position` at the start of `add_client` would actually be wrong: after waiting several seconds, the frozen `min_start_at` would be in the past and the device wouldn't have enough lead time to connect and fill its output buffer.

The re-collect after the wait uses the same `time.time()` as the predicate's last evaluation (same event loop iteration, lock held), so there's no meaningful gap between them.

I guess we could preserve the old deviceID for existing installs by reading it out of the legacy player config during migration and keeping it around but it would mean two ID shapes coexisting (legacy = deviceID, new = host:port), which is doable but adds a bit of complexity to carry forward.

Given the only thing that I think would actually break is universal groups containing a Fully Kiosk player, and my guess is that is not that likely that many users would have that, I figured a one-time re-link was the lighter trade-off. body:
This one is for the entire controller :) :

**API command function names**
We should keep the naming of api_commands consistent with the rest of the codebase, so `get_<thing>` or `list_<thing>`. So instead of
```
@api_command("audio_analysis/analyzed_tracks")   
async def analyzed_tracks(
```
we should use
```
@api_command("audio_analysis/analyzed_tracks")
async def get_analyzed_tracks(
```

**AA models**
Let's add a couple of dataclasses to the [models package](https://github.com/music-assistant/models). This will allow us to easily work with them and create/generate a frontend interface to populate on the frontend side. These models should really represent what we want to show in the frontend, not necessarily the database row. So for example, I feel we could drop unnecessary info such as `provider_loaded: True` from the `status` function. Have a look at the DSP models in the models package for some inspiration.

**Pagination**
Pagination is handled automatically by the websocket client if we use an AsyncGenerator. Have a look at [`playlist.tracks`](https://github.com/music-assistant/server/blob/75c6c18f0b42f88370dcbd0e801744cb095d72c5/music_assistant/controllers/media/playlists.py#L151) or [`iter_library_items`](https://github.com/music-assistant/server/blob/75c6c18f0b42f88370dcbd0e801744cb095d72c5/music_assistant/controllers/media/base.py#L308) how to do this

author: marcelveldt
body: Not an issue in MA's group architecture: only one player_id hits `serve_queue_item_stream` per group. For `sync_group`, `play_media` is dispatched to the sync leader only ([sync_group/player.py:343](../blob/feat/audio-sources/music_assistant/providers/sync_group/player.py#L343)) — members follow the leader's stream via DLNA/AirPlay-native sync. For `universal_group`, members hit the separate `/ugp/{player_id}.flac` endpoint, not `/single/` ([universal_group/player.py:272](../blob/feat/audio-sources/music_assistant/providers/universal_group/player.py#L272)) — only the UGP machinery itself consumes the queue item stream. So `on_source_selected` fires once per group, with the player_id of the consumer that actually streams the bytes, which is the right input to the plugin's player-switch logic.

author: marcelveldt
body: The wrapper does not use `contextlib.suppress` — the producer exception is logged with full traceback via `LOGGER.exception("AudioSource producer task raised")` in the finally ([helpers/audio.py:391-394](../blob/feat/audio-sources/music_assistant/helpers/audio.py#L391-L394)). Operators see the failure in the log; re-raising from a finally would shadow the outer stream's own exception flow (and the consumer has already exited by then, since the producer's own finally pushes the `b""` sentinel before the exception propagates to the task). Intentional behaviour.

author: marcelveldt
body: Already addressed in this exact shape: the `raise NotImplementedError` is BEFORE the `yield b""`, so the yield is unreachable and no stray empty chunk is emitted ([models/plugin.py:109-113](../blob/feat/audio-sources/music_assistant/models/plugin.py#L109-L113)). The yield is only there to keep Python's frame classification as an async generator so unimplemented providers fail deterministically on first iteration — exactly the behaviour requested. body: Fixed in [0752e49dd](../commit/0752e49dd). All four providers with a custom get_audio_stream (yandex_ynison, ariacast, vban, demo template) now snapshot `_active_session_id` at stream start alongside `_in_use_by_queue` and guard both the loop break-condition AND the finally release on both still matching. Same-queue reconnect updates the session id, so stream #1's loop exits the moment stream #2 takes over and its finally is a no-op — the new session's claim is preserved. FakePluginProvider in the contract tests mirrors the pattern, and the new `test_get_audio_stream_finally_does_not_clobber_reconnected_claim` regression walks the exact race.

author: OzGav
body:
I don't believe this is correct — the fallback Copilot is asking for is already in place. Walking through the relevant lines:
  
```
  487:    queue = self._queues[queue_id]
  488:    if not queue.current_item:
  489:        raise QueueEmpty("Cannot set playback speed: queue is empty")
  490:    queue_item_id = queue_item_id or queue.current_item.queue_item_id
  491:    queue_item = self.get_item(queue_id, queue_item_id)
  492:    if not queue_item:
  493:        raise InvalidDataError(f"Queue item {queue_item_id} not found in queue")
```

  - Line 488–489 guards that `queue.current_item` exists, so the attribute access on line 490 is safe.
  - Line 490 is exactly the default Copilot is suggesting: when the caller omits `queue_item_id` (it arrives as `None`), `None `or `queue.current_item.queue_item_id` evaluates to the `current item's id. get_item(..., None)` is never called.
  - Line 491 then runs against a resolved, non-None id.

  The "current item update check" further down also already uses the resolved id, not the original parameter:

  `507:    if queue.current_item and queue.current_item.queue_item_id == queue_item_id:
`
By the time we hit line 507, `queue_item_id` has been rebound on line 490, so the check correctly fires for the default (no-arg) case.

So both halves of the suggestion are already implemented. Happy to revisit if I've missed something specific, but as written the function does not call `get_item(..., None)` and does not error when `queue_item_id` is omitted.

After looking into it I believe I can move everything into the provider except one thing. The collapse migration deletes the legacy per-device provider instances, and that instance was the only link between a device ID (the old player_id) and its host. The legacy player config only stores password/SSL, so afterwards nothing can tell the provider which old device-id maps to the new `fully_kiosk_{host}_{port}` id.

So the only bit left in `config.py` is capturing that old to new map and handing it to the provider, which does all the actual rewriting. If you'd rather keep `config.py` completely clean, the alternative is to drop the remap entirely and just accept that the rare user with a universal group containing a Fully Kiosk player will need to re-add it.

author: OzGav
body:
Do not agree in fact I have gone a different way after looking into the the code further.

The whole-sync safety net already exists as the scan wraps every file in a try/except, so an unhandled error here never crashes the sync; it just skips that one file, which then gets retried on the next scan (the checksum is only stored on a successful import).

That retry-on-next-scan behaviour is actually what we want for transient failures. If a file has MBIDs and the lookup fails because MusicBrainz is briefly unreachable, falling back to tag-parsed names would import degraded data and store the checksum. So the file would be skipped on future scans and the good data would be lost until the file itself changes. Skipping and retrying later preserves the chance to get it right.

So the distinction is permanent vs. transient:
- InvalidDataError (bad/missing MBID means retrying won't help) return None, fall back to tag names.
- Transient errors (RetriesExhausted, transport/HTTP errors) let them propagate so the file is retried next scan.

This also matches the existing convention in this module (`get_artist_metadata` only catches `InvalidDataError`). I've simplified the method to only catch `InvalidDataError `and dropped the `RetriesExhausted `handling accordingly.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
**Blocking I/O on the event loop.** `tail.tail(...)` performs synchronous file I/O (`path.open("rb")`, `fh.seek`, `fh.read`) up to `_MAX_SCAN_BYTES = 10 MB` in `debug/log_reader.py:181-204`, but it's called directly from this `async def` tool. On a Home Assistant Yellow / Pi with slow eMMC or SD, 10 MB of seek+read will stall MA's single event loop hundreds of ms.

Same concern at `health_summary` (`tools/debug.py:581`), which calls `SafeLogTail(mass).count_errors_last_5min()` synchronously — that internally calls `tail(lines=2000, ...)` and can hit the same byte cap.

Suggested fix:

```python
return await asyncio.to_thread(
    tail.tail,
    lines=lines,
    level=level,
    component_regex=component_regex,
    since_seconds=since_seconds,
    name=name,
)
```

and similarly wrap the `count_errors_last_5min()` call in `health_summary`.

Done as suggested. A no-match result is now stored at `analysis_version` = -1, so the track keeps getting re-offered, and the provider declines the session in `start_analysis` while it's still inside the `retry_after` window. Thus it's not re-fingerprinted until the cooldown passes. All the retry logic is isolated in the AcoustID provider now.

One supporting change was needed to make the -1 actually get re-offered: the background-scan candidate query was selecting purely on row existence, so any stored row (including the -1 one) excluded the track. I made it version-aware so a track is offered for a domain when it has no row, or its row's `analysis_version` is below that domain's current version. It keys off the `analysis_version` column only, and it's no problem for the other providers today since none of them store rows below their current version.

body:
One last thing is in the exception handling. `AMPLIPI_API_ERRORS` won’t catch an unreachable controller as `pyamplipi` makes its calls with `aiohttp` but its except clauses only catch requests exceptions, which `aiohttp` never raises, so `AmpliPiUnreachableError` basically never fires. The raw `aiohttp` error comes through instead and your tuple doesn’t include it. That means a bad host at setup throws an uncaught error instead of `SetupFailedError`, and if the controller drops off the network the poll loop dies and never recovers.

Quick fix:
```
import aiohttp
AMPLIPI_API_ERRORS = (AmpliPiError, aiohttp.ClientError, TimeoutError, ValidationError, KeyError)

```

Worth raising the requests vs aiohttp issue upstream with pyamplipi too, but no need to block this PR on it. `ValidationError` and `KeyError` are both correct by the way, `model_validate` and the `response[‘sources’]` lookups do raise those.

author: OzGav
body:
Firstly, I have tightened the code generally. 

Secondly, thanks for the bigger picture. Full disclosure, I'm not familiar with UGP, squeezelite, or MultiClientStream so I can't really judge which is best between folding into MultiClientStream or making this the new shared helper. I think that is a discussion for you and Marvin?

On the dynamic-player-by-URL model I can think of a few questions such as: what does the device get on first connect with an empty queue; whether persisted entries stick in player settings (marked unavailable like other offline players) or get aged out; whether the queue is reachable for pre-listener curation when no listener has been around recently; how the URL's codec extension and any stored codec preference reconcile; and whether anything guards against URL hits creating state unintentionally.

Given those open questions I'd lean toward keeping the explicit-config model for now as it matches how other player providers work and avoids the lifecycle and persistence questions. The downside though is that it doesn't unlock the "any HA media player can play MA content by URL" capability your bigger vision points at and that needs the dynamic approach.

I'm happy for the bigger restructure to be your call. If you think this PR is a useful starting point that can be refactored later, we could add it basically as-is and let you drive the bigger plan as a follow-up. If you'd rather it be done first,  you'd need to steer me onto the target.

author: OzGav
body:
The main concern here, the dedup race, is already handled in this branch. The timestamp is now stamped before the await rather than after, so a   concurrent queue controller refresh sees a fresh timestamp during the callback window and skips, which avoids the double fetch. That matches how the queue controller already claims the slot before scheduling its own refresh.

On the suggestion to also throttle or swallow failures with a broad catch-all: I have left that out on purpose. The loop already catches the expected failure modes for a network metadata fetch (client errors, timeouts and our own MusicAssistantError) and keeps the monitor alive for those. Anything outside that set is treated as a real bug and is allowed to propagate, which is consistent with how we handle these provider callbacks elsewhere and with the teardown change in this same PR that awaits the monitor task and logs an unexpected exception when the stream ends. Adding a blanket except here would actually undo that, since the monitor would never surface those crashes.

If a specific unexpected exception turns out to recur in practice, the right fix is to add that type to the existing tuple rather than catch everything.

author: OzGav
body: Agreed, applying this. The monitor only catches a few expected error types, so any other exception ends the task. If that happens mid-stream, the task is already done by teardown and the current not done() check skips it, which is what leaves the exception unretrieved and logs the "Task exception was never retrieved" warning. Always awaiting it fixes that. Cancellation stays quiet (CancelledError is suppressed separately) and unexpected errors get logged instead of masking the original streaming error.

body:
**This breaks unauthenticated / protocol-triggered playback.**

`play_media` now wraps every call in `ImpersonatedUser`, and this raises `InsufficientPermissions` whenever there's no authenticated user in context — even when no `username` is passed. So hardware presets (squeezelite) and Spotify Connect / Plex / AirPlay handoffs (`play_media(queue_id, uri)` with no auth) will now fail. The suite doesn't catch it because `play_media` is mocked everywhere. Confirmed at runtime: `ImpersonatedUser(mass, None)` with `current_user=None` raises.

Fix: only require auth when actually impersonating *another* user; a call with no `username` and no auth should be a no-op (anonymous playback). Verified this keeps the existing context-manager test green.

(Also: this message and the `__init__` docstring still say `OptionalImpersonatedUser` / `UseImpersonatedUser` — class is `ImpersonatedUser`.)

```suggestion
        if authenticated_user is None:
            # No authenticated user in context (e.g. playback from a hardware
            # button or an external protocol). Impersonating another user is not
            # allowed, but a call without a username is a no-op so anonymous
            # playback keeps working.
            if username is not None:
                raise InsufficientPermissions(
                    "Authentication is necessary to impersonate another user."
                )
            return
        if username is not None:
            if (
                authenticated_user.role != UserRole.ADMIN
                and authenticated_user.username != self.username
            ):
                raise InsufficientPermissions("Can only impersonate another user as Admin.")
        else:
            self.username = authenticated_user.username
```

author: marcelveldt
body:
Paired with the `__init__` change above: when there's no user to impersonate, `self.username` stays `None`, so `__aenter__` should no-op instead of asserting. Also renamed the walrus var so it no longer shadows the module-level `impersonated_user` ContextVar.

```suggestion
        if self.username is None:
            # no-op: nothing to impersonate (no authenticated user, no username)
            return self
        if user := await self.mass.webserver.auth.get_user_by_username(self.username):
            set_impersonated_user(user)
            return self
        raise InvalidDataError(f"A user with user id or name {self.username} is not available.")
```

author: marcelveldt
body:
Thanks for jumping on this 🙏

One thing though — I don't think this fully closes the leak yet. `is_allowed_redirect_url()` is a three-way classifier: it returns `(True, "external")` for any valid-but-unknown external URL (anything that isn't same-origin / localhost / private IP / base_url / a registered pattern). Since we only check `is_valid` here, a `return_url` like `https://evil.com` still passes and we still append the token to it — which is exactly the vector the advisory describes.

`_handle_auth_authorize` gets away with the `is_valid`-only check because it never appends the token (that happens later in `_handle_auth_callback`, which gates `external` behind a consent screen). This endpoint appends the token immediately and has no consent step, so it should only auto-redirect to `trusted` destinations:

```suggestion
                # SECURITY FIX (GHSA-j369-4c4w-7qmq): only forward the token to trusted
                # destinations. is_allowed_redirect_url returns (True, "external") for any
                # unknown external URL, so checking is_valid alone still leaks the JWT.
                _, category = is_allowed_redirect_url(return_url, request, self.base_url)
                if category != "trusted":
                    return web.Response(status=400, text="Invalid return_url")
```

All the legit callers (web UI = same-origin, app = `musicassistant://`, HA = `homeassistant.local` / `my.home-assistant.io`, LAN = private IP) already resolve to `trusted`, so this shouldn't break any real flow.

Could you also add a quick regression test asserting an external/blocked `return_url` is rejected and the token isn't appended? Would've caught this, and it protects the backport.

So we have two approaches, current plugin model or core functionality model. I think they're optimising for different users, not the same problem expressed two different ways. I think plugin is simpler UX for a dumb internet radio in the kitchen as the user sets up the stream, gets shown the URL required, and enters that into the device. Dynamic-URL is essential for the "any HA media_player plays MA content via URL" capability you outlined and I don't think that's achievable any other way. That feels bigger than this PR and like it'd benefit from your architectural call before I build. Two main questions: Does the URL-addressable-queue idea belong as core MA infrastructure (sub-controller of streams), or as a provider? If infrastructure, is now the right time to commit, or would you prefer the explicit provider lands now and we revisit later? author: marcelveldt
body:
This is where it goes wrong. The producer dumps the whole decoded buffer into the queue in a burst (buffer is 60-1200s, worker drains at ~5x), so for basically any track longer than the queue depth the queue is full at EOF and this `None` gets dropped. The worker then drains its backlog and blocks forever on `queue.get()` — the session is never popped and the cancel callbacks don't fire (EOF was received) — so the worker leaks. That's the *only* reason `_finalize_session` needs a timeout at all.

Reliably deliver the terminator instead (single-threaded, no await in between, so race-free):

```python
if is_last_chunk:
    finalized = True
    if queue.full():
        with contextlib.suppress(asyncio.QueueEmpty):
            queue.get_nowait()  # evict one chunk so the sentinel always lands
    queue.put_nowait(None)
    self.mass.create_task(_finalize_session())
    return
```

Then the worker always terminates on its own and `_finalize_session` can go back to a plain `await worker`.

Ah, I had not thought of using an API call to do this. That clears up some of my concerns.

If dynamic creation is triggered by an API call rather than by an HTTP request hitting an open URL, then:

- Nothing is created accidentally, only when something explicitly asks for it.
- HA will have already added what it wants to play before the device connects, so the queue is never empty at first connect. That removes the silence question entirely.
- The temporary players don't need persisted settings since they're explicitly throwaway.
- The permanent players keep working the way they do today with the same UI, same setup, same URL copy-paste.

A few things to check:

- I think the extra concepts you are talking about would be additive to this PR so is it an option to merge what's on the branch now, with temporary players and the API command as a follow-up PR? Smaller pieces, easier to review?
- On the name, "Web Player" works for me in principle, I also thought of "Web Broadcast"?
- I'm already using a multi-value stations `ConfigEntry` (one name per line, each becomes a player). Is that the setup you had in mind for the permanent list?

As for extra help I'm happy with anything you have the capacity to provide!

author: marcelveldt
body:
I now understand the problem you're facing better.

- when playing content from a streaming provider (e.g. an album, playlist) we already have the (minimal) track data available so unless the data is too minimal, we don't call the get_track endpoint to save API calls
- at time of playback the track data is available to us but we throw it away and only store the id's in the playlog table

- if you later want to query that playlog table again (which can be reconstructed into simple ItemMapping objects), you will know what item played but none of the metadata is there, including the artist(s) or album of a track

- Doing a get_item or get_track call to resolve the item for the lastfm provider will result in a bunch of api calls so if possible to avoid we should do so. Unless we think this is very limited and like you said will only be once as the data is cached after that. But if the lastfm plugin is quering different tracks all the time that won't be good.

Idea 1:
Write the track object to cache if it's already complete. A bit fragile as you do not exactly know the cache category/key per provider so you may want to write it into some special bucket.

Idea 2:
Write the artist and album to the playlog table (maybe as json objects?)

Idea 3:
Just accept the calls if we can guarantee that it will be a limited number.

Thanks. I don't think idea 3 is the solution when we have ideas 1 and 2. Personally I prefer idea 2 as I feel it is the neatest and that data may prove useful in the future as it will be available to all.

Idea 1 can work and I was thinking of something like writing the artist (and album) into a dedicated cache bucket at mark_item_played time, only when we already have the data in hand and only when this provider is loaded so we don't store for nothing:

```
# in mark_item_played, gated on the lastfm_recommendations provider being loaded
await self.mass.cache.set(
    key=f"{media_item.provider}.{media_item.item_id}",
    data={"artist": ..., "album": ...},  # data we already have, no extra fetch
    category=CACHE_CATEGORY_RECENT_PLAY_ARTISTS,  # our own bucket
    expiration=3600 * 24 * 30,
)
```

The seed resolution would then read from our own bucket and falls back to `get_library_item_by_provid` (DB only) skipping if neither hits. Using our own category also sidesteps the fragility you mentioned about not knowing each provider's cache key/category as we're not touching the providers' `get_track` buckets, just our own.

Having said that, I still lean towards idea 2 for the durability/reuse reasons above. Happy to go whichever way you think fits best.

body: Deliberate choice. The toolset (`filters.py`) owns its vocabulary and imports nothing from the package, keeping the dependency graph acyclic; moving `ShelfType` into `models.py` would flip that and couple the toolset to the plan models instead. The plan stays renderer-agnostic in the sense that matters: it owns no bytes and no filter strings. An alternative renderer would dispatch on the enum members (`LOW`/`HIGH`) — the ffmpeg-named values are just a convenience for this renderer.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body: Intentional trade-off. The attack surface of this finding is API-supplied path strings (item_id / browse path / playlist name) — nothing in the API can create symlinks. Anyone able to plant a symlink inside the base directory already has filesystem access on the host, so a symlink-following check adds no protection against the actual threat. Symlinks inside the base are admin-created and legitimate; a realpath-based check would reject those setups and also reintroduce blocking IO on the event loop (this helper runs in per-track hot paths, including SMB/NFS mounts), which is exactly why the earlier realpath version was replaced.

author: MarvinSchenkel

See the reply on the helper for the full rationale.

body: This can't happen in practice: aiosqlite enqueues the commit to its worker thread synchronously (put_nowait before the first await point), so once the finally block runs the COMMIT is guaranteed to execute - cancelling the awaiting task only abandons the result, it doesn't prevent the commit. A shield would just add an extra task per scope exit without changing the outcome.

body:
The suggested code has a flaw: if the runner task fails with an exception, `.result()` re-raises it outside the except `TimeoutError` block, so it escapes as a raw exception instead of a `SetupFailedError` which means the loader won't schedule a retry. That's the exact problem this PR fixes.

The scenario it guards against is also mostly unreachable as `get_config_entries` probes for a usable snapserver binary and defaults to external-server mode when there isn't one. And if snapserver crashes before logging its version line, the runner exits cleanly rather than raising, so the fail-fast wouldn't trigger the way the suggestion assumes. Worst case today is a one-off 30 second wait in a background task before failing with a clean, retryable error which is not worth the extra complexity.

author: OzGav
body:
OK this is confirmed real. I reproduced it by syncing audiobooks from an actual Google Drive account: every file failed with Cloud path not found: http:... because the chapter scan passed the URL-derived parent_path into `_scandir`.

The root cause is older than this PR though. `FileSystemItem.parent_path` derives from `absolute_path`, but `_scandir` (and `exists/_read_file`) take relative paths. Most call sites already use `relative_parent_path`, and the handful of audiobook/podcast ones that didn't only worked on local providers because `os.path.join` with an absolute second argument happens to be a no-op. The WebDAV provider already had to add URL-to-relative conversion workarounds for the same reason.

Fixed by making relative paths the single currency: the remaining call sites now use `relative_parent_path`, `parent_name` is derived from the relative path, and the now-unused `parent_path` property is removed (it had no other consumers). Behaviour is unchanged for local/SMB/NFS/WebDAV, and audiobook sync from Google Drive now works and was verified before/after with a multi-file audiobook. Added a regression test covering parent-folder scans on cloud items.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
[PROBLEM] This playlog join can fan out: without a session user (the normal case for a scheduled sync) rows for *all* users match, and `get_library_item_sync_details` runs with `limit=1` and no `ORDER BY`, so SQLite returns an arbitrary resume-state row. The `base_query` above guards against exactly this with a correlated subquery (`ORDER BY p2.timestamp DESC LIMIT 1` — "so the join can never fan out the result set"). In a multi-user install with divergent resume positions this either triggers a spurious `update_item_in_library` on every sync (defeating the optimization) or skips a genuine resume-state change, depending on which row wins. Suggest mirroring the base_query join:

```sql
LEFT JOIN playlog ON playlog.id = (
    SELECT p2.id FROM playlog p2
    WHERE p2.item_id = audiobooks.item_id AND p2.media_type = 'audiobook'
    [AND p2.userid = :playlog_userid]
    ORDER BY p2.timestamp DESC LIMIT 1)
```

author: MarvinSchenkel
body: [PROBLEM] This heal trusts the stale parent link, but nothing ever clears the persisted `protocol_parent_id` when a player registers with a *non-protocol* type (the native branch of `_evaluate_protocol_links` never touches it; `update_state` only re-persists the type). So a genuine protocol→player conversion (e.g. `_save_underlying_player_id`'s "bridge client turned web player") persists as `player_type: "player"` + stale link — exactly the pattern healed here. Result: every restart flips the type to `protocol` (hiding the player from the config API until it re-registers — indefinitely if the device is offline) and registration flips it back, with no convergence; while mistyped, `_recover_cached_protocol_links` also re-adopts it as a phantom output on the old parent. Suggest clearing the persisted parent link when a player registers with a non-protocol type, or only healing when the parent's `linked_protocol_ids` also references the child.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body: [PROBLEM] `get_track_lyrics` (metadata/controller.py:328) loops over lyrics providers with no error handling, so a transient LRCLIB failure (5xx/network, or `RetriesExhausted` — `@throttle_with_retries` only retries `ResourceTemporarilyUnavailable`, not `ClientResponseError`) now aborts the loop, skipping remaining lyrics providers such as genius_lyrics, and propagates out of the API command instead of the previous graceful "no lyrics". Suggest wrapping the per-provider call in `get_track_lyrics` in the same try/except-and-continue pattern this PR added in enrichment.py.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body: [PROBLEM] This short-circuit assumes alias→genre resolution is static, but it changes over time: a user can create a new genre whose name/alias matches an already-stored alias, and the daily scan grows aliases via `_ensure_aliases`. Previously the next sync re-resolved every alias and `to_add` created the new mapping; now the sync returns early because the alias *strings* are unchanged, so the mapping is never created via sync. The compensating `_bulk_scan_unmapped_genres` only resolves names from items' `metadata.genres` JSON — names delivered via `get_item_genre_names` aren't guaranteed to be there, so those items can be permanently skipped. Consider invalidating the short-circuit when the genre/alias set changed since the mappings were written (e.g. compare against `max(timestamp)` of the genres table captured per sync run).

author: MarvinSchenkel

body: True in theory, but this only affects requests that are in-flight at the exact moment the hourly window rolls over - they write (nearly) identical timestamps and the next read sees the fresh value again. author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
[CRITICAL] Playlist track resolution is broken on cloud providers: the inherited `_parse_playlist_line` (filesystem_local `__init__.py`) builds its first candidate via `Path(self.get_absolute_path(playlist_path)) / line).resolve()`, which joins onto `base_path` (= the opaque folder ID, a relative string) and resolves against the server process CWD. Cloud `resolve()` then raises `MediaNotFoundError`, but the candidate loop only does `contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError)`, so the exception escapes to the outer `except MusicAssistantError` and no further candidate is tried - including root-relative lines that would have resolved. Every m3u/pls entry fails.

Reproduced against this PR's own `_StubCloudProvider` (tree contains `Artist/track.mp3`):

```python
>>> await provider._parse_playlist_line("track.mp3", "Artist")
result: None
warning: Could not parse track.mp3 to track: Cloud path not found: Users
```

Note the mangled `Users/...` path - the CWD leaked in and resolution stopped there.

WebDAV hit this exact issue and fixed it by overriding `_parse_playlist_line` (webdav/provider.py), joining relative to the playlist folder with `posixpath.normpath` and suppressing `(FileNotFoundError, MediaNotFoundError)`. `CloudFileSystemProvider` needs the same override (or better: make the local implementation relative-path based, like this PR already did for `parent_path`, and let webdav drop its copy). Please also add a regression test - the suite covers artwork/lyrics/audiobook siblings but not playlist entries.

author: marcelveldt
body:
One thing that popped in my head a couple of times (and its actually a model we had in the code years ago) is to simply put everything we see come across the wire in the library db - just none of their provider mappings have "in_library" set to true so it basically means it is just there for reference. I wont show up in any listing, its just there as a placeholder with whatever data we had at the moment we saw this item

When the item later gets added to the library, the metadata fulfill request kicks in and will complement the data.
The harsh truth however is that many streaming providers only provide very limited metadata in their listings results (so playlist tracks, album tracks etc.) which makes sense from a data hygiene and performance aspect, we actually do the same with our list results.

The other downside of this is that you start filling the library db with tracks you may never ever see again, meaning unbounded growth with items that are not the main interest. It does however help a ton with resolving cases like this. If we ever saw this item in any result, we have its data "cached", ready to use without needing to do an api call to get the full data.

An alternative is that we smartly use the cache db for this (which has expiry builtin) to quickly store these items for later use but I have not yet seen a clear model how we can ever get that implemented in a clean way without hacks. Also, going back to what I said above about the "list" items being just compact variants of these media items, they are probably lacking the metadata we care about anyways so we can wonder if this is all worth it.

So for now (until we ever have some global cache for all MA users) the stance still is that we should be very careful in making too many calls to streaming providers (or metadata providers). A quick win for now could just be that you try a fetch in the library first - if that does not deliver you any results at all, you do a small batch of resolving provider items.

For example whenever you try to do a "get_track" on a spotify track, you are within their rate limiter. While you are doing these calls, the user will not be able to do a search, fetch the contents of an album, playlist etc.  and it can even impact audio playback if the rate limiter really kicks in.


Hope you get my point

body:
`_stamp_qr_on_cover()` does a synchronous PIL decode + resize + PNG re-encode of a 512px cover, running directly on the event loop on every cache miss. MA's own image code offloads all PIL work to a thread (see the `asyncio.to_thread` calls throughout `music_assistant/helpers/images.py`). Since this same server also streams audio on that loop, a burst of TV requests right after a QR rotation (new cache key) will stall playback for every connected player while each composite runs.

Suggest offloading:
```python
cached = await asyncio.to_thread(_stamp_qr_on_cover, cover_bytes, qr_buf.getvalue())
```
The `segno.make(...).save(...)` calls are lighter but could ride along in the same thread hop.

author: MarvinSchenkel

author: MarvinSchenkel

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
Both behaviors are intentional; clarified the first in the docstring (cdafea9).

- A match near the deadline still gets its confirmation hold on purpose: bounding the hold by the remaining timeout would reject a late-but-real playback start, which is strictly worse than holding the group lock ~2s longer. The total wait is bounded at `timeout + stable_for` — the docstring now states the wait may exceed `timeout` by one hold.
- The end-of-hold check (instead of monitoring throughout) is deliberate: the consumer of this wait reads the player state once after the lock is released, so the value at the end of the hold is exactly what matters. A value that flips off and back on during the hold ends up matching — the correct answer for the resume gate that follows. Continuous monitoring would add complexity without changing any decision.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
The mechanism is described correctly (a mid-hold transient leaves the event set, so the next wait returns immediately and another hold runs), but the bound is not exceeded: every hold is gated by the deadline check before it can start, so any number of holds consume the timeout budget rather than extend it — only the final hold can cross the deadline, keeping the total at `timeout + stable_for` as documented.

Requiring a *fresh* matching update per hold would introduce a real miss: a value that flaps off at the end of one hold but stabilizes back to the target during that same window has already emitted its last matching transition — clearing it and demanding a new one means no update ever comes and we'd time out on a genuinely stable value. The end-of-hold check reads live state, which is authoritative regardless of event bookkeeping, so the current form cannot miss; worst case is one wasted (bounded) hold in a pathological flap.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
**[PROBLEM] Empty `target_players` produces a discoverable but unplayable renderer.**

With the default config (`target_players` unset), the fallback renderer has `player_id=""`. A DLNA app can discover it and send `SetAVTransportURI`, but every `Play` is dropped right here (`return`), and the MA-UI path then fails in `get_stream_details` with "no active stream". So out-of-the-box the provider advertises a device that can never play — while the config help text says "Leave empty for a single renderer without a fixed target", implying it works.

Suggest defaulting empty → `*`, making a target required, or clearly documenting that a target must be configured.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
**[PROBLEM] Pause→Play restarts the stream from 0 instead of resuming.**

Every DLNA `Play` action runs `_on_play`, which always calls `play_media(target, source_uri, option=QueueOption.PLAY)` and resets `inst.elapsed_offset = 0` above. When a control point sends `Play` to resume after `Pause`, this re-initiates playback (upstream re-fetched from byte 0) and resets the displayed elapsed time to zero, rather than resuming the paused MA player. For file-based pushes (e.g. foobar2000 pushing a FLAC) this restarts the track.

Fix: capture the prior `transport_state` in the renderer's Play handler (renderer.py:330, before it is overwritten to `PLAYING`); if it was `PAUSED_PLAYBACK`, call `cmd_play(target)` instead of `play_media`.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
Connections don't actually accumulate here: `_dashboard_connections` is keyed by `device_id`, so a repeated failed `show_dashboard` to the same device reuses the cached entry (or replaces it if the socket dropped) — it's bounded to one per device, never stacking. It's also cleaned up by `hide_dashboard` and on `unload`.

The only real gap is that an on-demand connect that then times out on app launch leaves one live socket cached for a device showing nothing until the next hide/unload — bounded and rare. Worth noting the naive "disconnect on failure" is unsafe: `_get_or_create_chromecast` can return an *active player's* `cc`, so a blanket teardown would kill a live audio player. Leaving as-is for now given it's bounded and self-heals; will revisit with a `created`-flag guard if it proves noisy.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body: True in theory, but intentionally left unbounded: each queued task only holds the small parsed request dict — the heavy allocations (image bytes, hex string) happen after acquiring the semaphore, so those stay capped at 6. The only sender is the authenticated, certificate-pinned client, whose service worker is cache-first and only requests visible images, so there is no realistic flood source. Bounding the queue (or acquiring the semaphore before spawning) would either add machinery for a non-threat or reintroduce the receive-loop blocking this PR removes.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body: This window doesn't exist: in _close_data_channel_bridge, building the task snapshot, resetting the session fields and calling cancel() on every task is one synchronous block — no await until the first `await task`. On a single-threaded event loop the forward loop is parked at an await point that whole time; once cancel() is requested it wakes with CancelledError at that await and never reaches the spawn code again. The spawn itself (queue.get() → json.loads → create_task → add to proxy_tasks) is also synchronous, so a task can never be created without being in the set the snapshot sees.

Addressed in d4a425d68: `start_run` now holds a dedicated `self._session_lock` across the concurrency guards and the session insert.

To be precise about what this changed: it was not a live bug. There was no `await` between the guards and `self._sessions[session_id] = session`, so asyncio could not interleave two calls and the check-and-insert was already atomic. The problem was that the correctness rested on an invisible property of a ~65 line method -- adding an `await` in that span later would have silently opened the race.

Added a regression test covering two concurrent `start_run` calls. Note it passes with or without the lock today, precisely because the race is not reachable; it pins the observable contract so the guarantee breaks loudly if that span ever gains an await.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
**[CRITICAL] Switching the folder `provider` from `library` to `recommendations` changes every row's `uri`, which silently resets everyone's Discover page customization.**

`_MediaItemBase.__post_init__` derives `uri = create_uri(FOLDER, provider, item_id)`, so `library://folder/in_progress` becomes `recommendations://folder/in_progress`. The frontend keys the entire Discover page on that uri:

1. **Priority pins stop matching.** `HomeWidgetRows.vue` builds `availableRowIds` from `folder.uri` and only keeps a `DEFAULT_PRIORITY_ROWS` entry `if (recSet.has(id))`. `discoverRows.ts` hardcodes `library://folder/in_progress` and `library://folder/recently_played` there, so both pins are skipped and those two rows lose their fixed top slots.
2. **Hidden rows reappear.** `resolveDiscoverRowsConfig` filters the saved `hidden` list against the available ids, so every `library://folder/*` a user had hidden is dropped and the row renders again.
3. **Saved order resets** for these 11 rows — `mergeOrder(..., keepUnavailable=false)` drops the stale ids.

Nothing throws; users just find their Discover page reverted after upgrading. Combined with the interleave change below, In progress / Recently played also move from the top of the page to after every music provider's rows.

Two ways to close this:

- **Keep the uris stable** — `uri` is a plain field and `__post_init__` only fills it when `None`, so `_folder()` can pass `uri=f"library://folder/{item_id}"` explicitly. No frontend work, no migration; downside is the uri names a provider that no longer exists.
- **Companion frontend PR** — update `DEFAULT_PRIORITY_ROWS` and rewrite `library://folder/` -> `recommendations://folder/` when reading the saved `discover.rows` preference. Cleaner long-term, but the two repos have to land together.

Related: the checklist item _"For changes affecting the UI, the companion PR in `music-assistant/frontend` is linked"_ applies here and is currently unchecked.

Separately (non-blocking but same area): removing the explicit `library_rows()` prepend in the controller means builtin rows now come **last** in every interleave pass, because `get_providers_supporting_feature` tiers `PLUGIN` after `MUSIC` and `METADATA`. `test_rows_interleaved_builtin_first` only still passes because the monkeypatched provider list puts the recommendations provider first, which the real implementation does not.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
**[CRITICAL] Duplicating the 11 existing `common.media.recommendations.*` strings here makes all of them fall back to English for every non-English user.**

`_candidate_keys` tries the owner-namespaced key first, and `_lookup` falls back to `en.json` before the next candidate is tried — so the new `provider.recommendations.*` key wins over the already-translated `common.*` key. Verified against `de.json` on this branch:

```
owner "library"         -> de: common.media.recommendations.in_progress_items.name           = "Teilweise abgespielt"
owner "recommendations" -> en: provider.recommendations.media...in_progress_items.name       = "In progress"
```

That is 59 already-translated strings across 9 locales that go back to English until Lokalise round-trips the new keys.

Note that deleting the `common.media.recommendations.*` keys instead is not an option — three other providers reuse them and have no strings of their own, so they resolve purely through the owner -> common fallback:

- `audiobookshelf/constants.py:97` -> `in_progress_items`
- `nicovideo/provider_mixins/explorer.py:80,94` -> `recently_played`, `recent_favorite_tracks`
- `opensubsonic/sonic_provider.py:882,934` -> `recently_added_albums`

Suggested fix — the fallback already resolves the existing keys without any declaration, so:

1. Drop this whole `media.recommendations` block (keep `manifest.description`).
2. Add only the 5 genuinely new rows to `music_assistant/strings.json` under `media.recommendations`, next to their 11 siblings.
3. Regenerate: `uv run -m scripts.build_translations`

That keeps every existing translation, gives the new rows one canonical home, and leaves the shared keys working for the three providers above.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
False positive -- this is valid Python 3.14 syntax.

[PEP 758](https://peps.python.org/pep-0758/) makes the parentheses optional in `except` when there is no `as` clause. This repo is 3.14-only (`.python-version` is `3.14`, `requires-python = ">=3.14"`), and the module imports fine on 3.14.4.

It is also not hand-written: `ruff format` produced it. I originally wrote `except (ZoneInfoNotFoundError, ValueError):` and the project's own formatter removed the parentheses. The same unparenthesized form is already used elsewhere on `dev` -- `mass.py`, `apple_music/media.py`, `apple_music/setup_flow.py`, `neteasecloudmusic`, `yandex_smarthome` -- so it is the house style the formatter enforces.

The `test` job on this commit is green, which imports the module, so a `SyntaxError` on import would have failed CI.

Note this is the fourth time this has been raised on this PR; the earlier three were the same `except TypeError, ValueError:` pattern and were closed for the same reason.

author: marcelveldt
body:
Exceptions for tasks can sometimes bubble up in a somewhat strange fashion with asyncio. In your case you can see the error MusicProvider.get_audio_stream' was never awaited which means something crashed. The code was porbbaly still calling the get_audio_stream in your provider Sure that happened too when you had set the "direct" attribute of the streamdetails.

if you fill streamdetails with the "direct" attribute it means we're not going to intercept with the stream but just feed the url into ffmpeg directly and let that deal with it. we do that for mpeg dash streams for example and also for local files.

You can set the streamdetails.streamtitle if you want for the updated track details from that callback. But those are small finetune details later. First focus on getting playback working. I have no way to test this to know what is going on but its getting harder to follow now that we're also spinning up a webserver to grab the audio bits. I still dont get why we cant just replicate what that webserver is doing and do that directly but for now its maybe good to use this at starting point.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
I just did some tests and I can get audio within 2-3 seconds via the binary on the command line. E.g. this works flawlessly: `yt-dlp -vU -o - "https://www.youtube.com/embed/5GD4hsz9W78" | vlc -`. The binary also seems to cache ciphers and signatures, judging by the logs. 

HOWEVER. This seems to work regardless of being logged in to YTM, which means that this approach enables using this provider for free, which is not something we want. Let's try the following:

1. Check whether we can figure out if the user has a Youtube Premium account. Then we can actively block using YTM if they are not paying for YTM.
2. If that works, we can embed the unix binary in MA and use a subprocess to obtain the stream url. We can extend the command above with some flags to automatically obtain the highest audio stream and probably can also configure it to only return the stream url instead of the bytes of the song.
3. If we cannot get it to return the stream url, we can stream the bytes back to MA which does require a tiny bit of refactoring. Spotify -> `get_audio_stream` is an example of this.

Looping in @marcelveldt to double check this approach.

> import yt_dlp
> 
> def _extract_stream_url(item_id):
>     ydl = yt_dlp.YoutubeDL()
>     info = ydl.extract_info(f"https://www.youtube.com/embed/{item_id}", download=False)
>     audio_only_formats = [
>         f
>         for f in info["formats"]
>         if f.get("audio_ext", "none") == "m4a" and f.get("video_ext", "none") == "none"
>     ]
>     # Formats are sorted from worse to better quality. Use the last/best one.
>     return audio_only_formats[-1]["url"]
> 
> print(_extract_stream_url("5GD4hsz9W78"))
> ```
> 
> So no need to use a subprocess. Using the CLI I don't think there is a way to get the streaming URL anyway.
> 
> Do you want to fully switch to yt-dlp? Or keep pytube around with an option to allow users to switch to that?
> 
> Regarding premium vs free I'll let you handle it. FWIW, I just tried the latest released version of Music Assistant on an account not subscribed to YTM Premium and surprisingly I could still play all the songs I tried.

Great find! Let's fully switch to yt-dlp 🚀 . In the mean time, I will figure out a way to actively block people without a YTM premium subscription.

One minor thing, instead of the custom code to figure out the audio stream, can we leverage the [format 'bestaudio' from yt-dlp](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp?tab=readme-ov-file#format-selection)? If that doesn't work, we can hook into a [custom format selector](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp?tab=readme-ov-file#use-a-custom-format-selector)

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
> I switched to using a format_selector with bestaudio.

author: MarvinSchenkel
body:
Let me first start off by saying 'Amazing work'. Really love the amount of detail you put into this PR.

I only really have one suggestion. Personally I think it makes sense to put the filter calculations inside the model classes themselves. This avoids quite some logic in the `audio.py` helper class. 

So, for example, instead of using an `Enum` for the `ParametricEQBandType`, we could change this to an actual class with a `get_filter(sample_rate)` function that calculates the filter for us:

```python
class PeakParametricEQBand:

  ....

  def get_filter(sample_rate: int) -> str:
    b0 = 1 + alpha * a
    b1 = -2 * math.cos(w_0)
    b2 = 1 - alpha * a
    a0 = 1 + alpha / a
    a1 = -2 * math.cos(w_0)
    a2 = 1 - alpha / a

    return f"biquad=b0={b0}:b1={b1}:b2={b2}:a0={a0}:a1={a1}:a2={a2}"
```

Then, in `audio.py` we can reduce all the logic to simply:
```python
...
# Process each DSP filter sequentially
  for f in dsp.filters:
      if not f.enabled:
          continue
  
      if isinstance(f, ParametricEQFilter):
          for b in f.bands:
              if not b.enabled:
                  continue

              filter = b.get_filter(sample_rate)
              filter_params.append(filter)
```

What do you and @marcelveldt think?

author: marcelveldt
body:
> What do you and @marcelveldt think?

I was kind of wondering the same - the models that we have defined in our separate repo/package are basically models that are shared between client and server (we handle serialization and some validation there as well) but these seem to be server-side models only, its pretty much self-contained data and logic. So yeah it could make sense to make these server side models (actual classes and not dataclasses) but you can even have a mix of both worlds, it perfectly fine to add some helper methods to the dataclasses, for instance to create this filter config with a simple helper method within the model class.

I'm fine either way but if this logic is server-side only I'd vote for moving them to the servercode instead of the shared models package.

author: marcelveldt
body:
> Have rebased and bumped the models package. Just need to figure out these last 2. Looks like all MediaControllerBase must take a MediaItemType, and that is not an ItemMapping? So should I assert that I have an Artist before calling update_item_in_library

Yeah, MediaControllerBase only take MediaItemType and that can never ever be an ItemMapping.
We only use ItemMapping for nested objects and incomplete/fast listings (such as search).
Now I did have a fair share of fighting with typing when I implemented that base class with the dynamic type inheritence so there may be something super stupid hidden inside it :-)

author: marcelveldt
body:
Darn yeah... Artist is an exception where we sometimes take ItemMapping - I believe that is done to prevent ourselves from having to query an entire chain of objects when we just want one track added to the lib. So we accept the ItemMapping, try to resolve it lazy and if not accept it as input as an artist object has no nested objects.

Long story short: The ArtistController takes an Artist or ItemMapping as input for the add and update methods

author: marcelveldt
body:
Ha creative but genius - yeah this is good, it keeps the strict typing (and hints). Nice work!
The easy way could indeed be to simply accept ItemMapping for the other objects as well just to satisfy typing but that will lead us into a giant shitshow if you try add an itemmapping to the lib or seomething like that. 

ItemMapping's are evil but we need them to be efficient :-)

Thanks!
